subject: biology
title: Limiting Factors Adventure
welcome_lead: Today you'll explore how light, CO₂ and temperature limit photosynthesis.
meta_desc: A-Level Biology Photosynthesis — limiting factors, compensation point, glasshouse strategies and the effect of temperature.
final_note: You learned that at any moment one factor (light, CO2 or temperature) limits photosynthesis, and that commercial growers manipulate these in glasshouses to maximise yield.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Photosynthesis needs light, CO₂ and warmth. Whichever is in shortest supply is the limiting factor.

Plot rate vs light intensity:
- Rises steeply at first (light limits)
- Then plateaus (something else limits — usually CO₂)
- Raising CO₂ moves the plateau up; raising temperature too

Plants also respire all the time. At dawn or dusk:

Compensation point = light intensity at which photosynthesis just equals respiration. Net gas exchange = 0.

- Above it → plant gains glucose
- Below it → plant respires net (uses stored glucose)

Shade plants have a lower compensation point than sun plants — they survive in dim conditions.

Temperature affects enzymes:
- Below ~10 °C: too cold, slow rate
- ~25–30 °C: optimum for many plants
- Above ~40 °C: RuBisCO denatures; stomata also close, limiting CO₂

Commercial glasshouses:
- Burn paraffin → adds CO₂ AND heat
- Artificial lighting extends day length
- Ventilation prevents overheating

By controlling all three factors, growers can double or triple yields.

options: Maximum rate of photosynthesis
Light intensity where photosynthesis equals respiration
Optimum temperature for RuBisCO
Saturation point for CO2

mcqs.q: Why might burning paraffin in a glasshouse boost photosynthesis?
options: It removes CO2
It adds CO2 and heat
It cools the plants
It produces light

mcqs.q: Where do plants get most of their biomass from?
options: From carbon dioxide in the air — the carbon in plant tissue comes mostly from CO2 fixed during photosynthesis.
Plants get most of their mass from the soil through their roots.
Plants gain most of their mass directly from sunlight, which has weight.
Plants only respire at night and only photosynthesise during the day; the processes never overlap.

mcqs.q: What happens to an enzyme when it is denatured?
options: Plants gain most of their mass directly from sunlight, which has weight.
The enzyme has been completely broken into amino acids.
The enzyme has died because enzymes are alive.
Its tertiary structure (3D shape) changes, particularly the active site, so it can no longer bind substrate effectively.
